transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Ever since that robbery I went through a couple of years ago, I keep organizing my whole life around avoiding anything that reminds me of it—certain neighborhoods, late meetings, even some community events. It has gotten to the point where I realize I'm arranging my entire life around just trying to feel safe.
Do you also experience flashbacks, nightmares, or intense distress when reminded of the robbery?

Yes, absolutely. If I hear a loud male voice or lock up an office, I will suddenly feel like I'm back on that floor with the gun at my head, and I can't catch my breath. I also lie awake replaying that night and wake up with my heart racing, while just the thought of being in a store or parking garage after dark makes my skin crawl.
Do you also find yourself constantly on edge, easily startled, or having trouble concentrating, even when you're not directly reminded of the robbery?

Yes, I feel like I'm constantly on watch, automatically checking for exits and scanning who comes in and out of a room wherever I go. If someone comes up behind me at work or a car door slams, I jump out of my skin and my heart just takes off. It takes me several minutes of shaking it off before I can even begin to focus again.

The persistence of symptoms since the robbery, their impact on daily functioning, and the specific triggers align with the criteria for F43.1 (Post-traumatic stress disorder). No new information contradicts this candidate, and no additional differential diagnoses are currently warranted based on the presentation.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent re-experiencing of a traumatic event (robbery), avoidance of trauma-related stimuli, negative alterations in mood and cognition, and marked hyperarousal symptoms, all lasting for more than one month and causing significant functional impairment. These meet full criteria for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, ICD-10 code F43.1.
